reading.body:
Defense AI procurement is documented in free federal databases, SAM.gov, USAspending, and FPDS, with the Defense Innovation Unit as the commercial entry point and subscription analysts layered on top.

The free sources are the primary record. SAM.gov lists solicitations and awards, USAspending carries every federal award, and FPDS records contract actions and vendor performance at the transaction level. DIU is where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings. Govini builds decision science on that record, and Silicon Valley Defense Group maps the commercial entrants.

The programs of record are decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing, the AI applications the sector tracks. Tracking them through procurement data shows actual spending and vendor capability, not just announcements. What the data does not show is compute demand, building capacity, or power requirements, none of those appear in these sources. Government AI labs are catalogued separately, not here.

summary: Decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing are the programs of record; DIU is the commercial on-ramp. Who tracks the sector: free government procurement databases are the primary record, with dedicated defense-intelligence firms layered on top - this page starts with the sources anyone can verify.

analysis.body:
The material assembled here does not include a measured adoption rate for AI in defense. There is no Census Bureau figure in this set, and no percentage of any kind appears in the excerpts, so nothing here supports a claim about how widely AI is deployed across the sector. What the sources do provide is the procurement and intelligence infrastructure through which defense AI spending can be observed and verified. A reader should treat this as a map of where evidence lives rather than as evidence of adoption itself.

That map starts with the federal procurement record. Per SAM.gov, the government's own system of record, contracting data searches cover contract opportunities, contract awards, and subcontract reports, and the site is where federal users now manage opportunity notices and contract award records. Per FPDS, the Federal Procurement Data System records contract actions at the transaction level, with detailed data elements documented including format, structure, requirements, and FAR references, and federal users manage award records using legacy FPDS credentials. USAspending is named as the place where every federal award is downloadable, though the harvested text from that page carries only the site name, so the detail behind it rests on this site's own description rather than on the page excerpt.

The record is also moving. Per SAM.gov, the General Services Administration has retired the Electronic Subcontracting Reporting System, with subcontracting reporting capabilities now available in SAM.gov, and the FPDS.gov ezSearch feature has been retired with all contract award data searches to be conducted in SAM.gov. Per SAM.gov and FPDS, the FPDS.gov ATOM Feed will be retired later in FY 2026. SAM.gov also notes that following revisions to the ISR eligibility logic within the Subcontracting Plan Reporting system on June 9, 2026, contractors might observe an increased volume of contracts and subcontracts in their Eligible Workspace, and that inclusion of these records does not automatically carry a further consequence. For anyone tracking AI-related defense awards, the practical point is that search habits built on the old systems need to change.

On the commercial side, the Defense Innovation Unit describes itself as the Department's innovation pointman, with a mission to convert entrepreneurial products into tangible combat power, and this site's curated point places it as where commercial AI enters DoD programs through public project listings. Govini is described in the material as building decision science on the procurement record, and its page language centers on a platform layer that transforms activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that proactively forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources, with readiness framed as a real-time condition that is continuously achieved. This site's description of Govini adds that it publishes public scorecards on critical-technology spending, a claim the harvested excerpt does not itself show.

The subscription analysts occupy a different layer. Per Janes, the company collects information from vetted on-the-ground and industry specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, describing these people as human sensors collecting data no web crawler could access, and it verifies every data point against vetted sources under strict credibility criteria. Janes states that it applies rigorous data governance and advanced technology to connect millions of data points, that final content is peer reviewed, and that its validated data and analysis inform the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. This site names Forecast International alongside Janes as a long-running defense analysis provider, but the harvested excerpt covers Janes only.

The government lab category is catalogued separately and is not a US defense vendor list. Per The World of AI's Government Labs page, two individually verified organisations are listed, the Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi, which operates under Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and has published frontier open models, and Shanghai AI Laboratory, which is backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government. The page notes that state-funded labs carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, and that both institutions can in principle command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.

On risk and posture, the material is mostly about handling rules rather than AI-specific regulation. Per SAM.gov, the system contains Controlled Unclassified Information, and anyone viewing, reproducing, or disposing of it must protect it in accordance with 32 CFR Part 2002 and GSA Order CIO 2103.2 CUI Policy, and the system is subject to monitoring with unauthorized activities subject to disciplinary action including criminal prosecution. No source here reports ROI evidence for defense AI deployments, and no source here reports a regulatory framework aimed specifically at military AI. One caution for the reader: the excerpt harvested from the Silicon Valley Defense Group page contains unrelated German-language recruitment text and does not show the company mapping described in this site's curated point, so that claim should be checked against the live page before it is relied on. For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the defensible path this material supports is to build the business case on the free federal procurement record, SAM.gov, FPDS, and USAspending, and to treat vendor and analyst claims as inputs to be verified against awards rather than as measured outcomes.

https://www.janes.com/.brief: Janes reports that it gathers information from vetted on-ground specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors that web crawlers cannot reach. Janes reports that every data point is verified against reliable, vetted sources and that its dataset is the largest of its type, connecting millions of points to uncover patterns. Janes reports that its final content is peer reviewed to meet its quality and accuracy standards, and that it supplies validated data for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Janes reports that its digital portal lets users navigate validated data to uncover insights, moving from “what happened” to “what it means.”

https://www.govini.com/.brief: Govini says that Air is a leader in Enterprise Readiness and that its mission is to make readiness a real-time, continuously achieved condition. The company explains that its platform layer turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The World of AI catalogues two organisations it classifies as government labs, each verified individually against a document the organisation published about itself, with the deciding source and the date it was last read recorded. It describes Shanghai AI Laboratory as a state-established Chinese research institution backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government, and says Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi operates under Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and has published frontier open models. The site argues that state-funded labs hold a distinct position because they carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, which shapes what they build. It adds that both entries, despite sharing the classification, represent very different political economies, and that both can in principle command infrastructure commitments such as compute and facilities that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.
